We look into the DAX Stock Index in Germany in this project. We look at the daily stock price for the DAX index for every day in 2025 from a time series analysis perspective, and we see how accurate we can make a model that predicts future values based off of its lags.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = pd.read_csv("data/DAX_2010-2020.csv")

data['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(data['Date'], format='%m/%d/%Y')

data = data.sort_values('Date')

data['Open'] = (
    data['Open']
    .str.replace('.', '', regex=False)
    .str.replace(',', '.', regex=False)
    .astype(float)
)

data.set_index('Date', inplace=True)


plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(data['Open'], label = "DAX Open")
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.ylabel('Price')
plt.title("DAX 2025 – Open Prices")
plt.show()

```

The data above shows roughly nonstationary data. We look at the autocorrelation function below to see how much lags depend on each other. In general, what we can tell is that the first point has a high correlation with the lags that follow. 


```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf



data = pd.read_csv("data/DAX_2010-2020.csv")

data['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(data['Date'], format='%m/%d/%Y')
data = data.sort_values('Date')

data['Open'] = (
    data['Open']
    .str.replace('.', '', regex=False)
    .str.replace(',', '.', regex=False)
    .astype(float)
)


data.set_index('Date', inplace=True)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
plot_acf(data['Open'], ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```

## ARMA 

Let's train a model to accurately reflect the data. First, let's try an autoregressive model - we notice that the model has lags that correlate well with the first 10, so, an autogregressive model should model it well. ARMA models do not work well with nonstationary data; we counter this with an ARIMA model that handles differencing. 


```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.arima_process import ArmaProcess
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

data = pd.read_csv("data/DAX_2010-2020.csv")

# Clean date
data['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(data['Date'], format='%m/%d/%Y')
data = data.sort_values('Date')

# Clean Open column
data['Open'] = (
    data['Open']
    .str.replace('.', '', regex=False)
    .str.replace(',', '.', regex=False)
    .astype(float)
)

data.set_index('Date', inplace=True)
data = data.asfreq('B')  # Business day frequency
data['Open'] = data['Open'].ffill()

returns = np.log(data['Open']).diff().dropna()

model = ARIMA(returns, order=(2,0,2))
result = model.fit()

sim = result.simulate(nsimulations=len(returns))

plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
plt.plot(returns.index, sim, label="ARMA(2,2) Simulation", color='blue')
plt.plot(returns.index, returns, label="Returns", color='yellow')
plt.legend()
```

We look at the AIC values of the ARMA models below. The smallest AIC value is -3961.6, for ARMA (3, 1).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\hline
 & MA(1) & MA(2) & MA(3) & MA(4) \\
\hline
AR(1) & -3965.5 & -3965.7 & -3972.9 & -3973.5 \\
AR(2) & -3962.0 & -3966.6 & -3972.8 & -3971.7 \\
AR(3) & -3961.6 & -3970.7 & -3974.7 & -3972.2 \\
AR(4) & -3972.8 & -3974.8 & -3972.4 & -3968.0 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{ARMA Model Comparison}
\label{tab:arma}
\end{table}

We graph an ARMA(3, 1) model below. It is not much different from ARMA(2, 2).

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.arima_process import ArmaProcess
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

data = pd.read_csv("data/DAX_2010-2020.csv")

# Clean date
data['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(data['Date'], format='%m/%d/%Y')
data = data.sort_values('Date')

# Clean Open column
data['Open'] = (
    data['Open']
    .str.replace('.', '', regex=False)
    .str.replace(',', '.', regex=False)
    .astype(float)
)

data.set_index('Date', inplace=True)
data = data.asfreq('B')  # Business day frequency
data['Open'] = data['Open'].ffill()

returns = np.log(data['Open']).diff().dropna()

model = ARIMA(returns, order=(3,0,1))
result = model.fit()

sim = result.simulate(nsimulations=len(returns))

plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
plt.plot(returns.index, sim, label="ARMA(3,1) Simulation", color='blue')
plt.plot(returns.index, returns, label="Returns", color='yellow')
plt.legend()
```
